parts.name: Passage 1
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

How to spot a liar?

A. However much we may abhor it, deception is common in nature. Some birds protect their young by feigning injury. They move away from their nests so that hungry predators follow them instead of attacking the nesting birds. Spider crabs use disguise. By adorning themselves with strips of kelp and other debris, they become difficult to see and can escape their enemies. Nature amply rewards successful deceivers because they survive long enough to reproduce. Humans also lie. According to psychologist Gerald Jellison of the University of Southern California, people are lied to about 200 times a day. Each untruth may have a purpose. People often deceive others to protect themselves or to gain something they cannot obtain in another way.

B. Detecting deceit can be just as important as telling a successful lie. Someone who recognises falsehood may avoid being swindled by an unscrupulous business associate or hoodwinked by a devious partner. There are several observable signs that can help people identify dissemblers. A liar’s account may become tangled when details do not match. Facial expressions, body language and tone of voice can also provide telltale evidence. In 2006, researchers Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo examined studies involving 24,483 judges. They found that people identified truths and lies correctly only 54 per cent of the time without special equipment or training. This shows that observing lying behaviour is possible, but not easy.

C. Good liars need to understand how other people feel. They must judge whether another person is suspicious, calm or convinced. The same skill is essential for people who try to detect lies. One important emotion to notice is stress. A person may feel stress when there is a conflict between the truth and what they are saying. However, stress alone does not prove that a person is lying. Someone may also feel nervous because they are frightened, embarrassed or under pressure. For this reason, lie detection usually depends on several signs rather than one movement or reaction.

D. Polygraphs are often called lie detectors, but they do not detect lies directly. They merely measure physical changes in the body while a person answers questions. A polygraph records respiration, heart rate and skin conductivity. These measures often increase when a person is nervous. Nervous people may perspire, and the salts in perspiration carry electricity. A sudden leap in skin conductivity may therefore suggest nervousness. The person may be worried about being caught while being economical with the truth. However, hot television studio lights could produce a similar reaction. This is one reason polygraph results are often inadmissible in court. Reliable observers therefore examine clusters of signs rather than depending on one physical reaction.

E. Many useful clues appear on the face. The musculature of the face is linked to parts of the brain involved in emotion. As a result, the countenance can show emotions before a person is able to hide them. In 1978, Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen published a system for classifying visible facial movements. Studies have suggested that genuine and insincere expressions are not always produced in the same way. For example, a patient paralyzed by a stroke on one side of the face may be asked to smile deliberately. In this case, only the mobile side of the mouth rises. However, when the patient hears a funny joke, a full and spontaneous smile may appear. This example shows that real emotion can affect facial movement automatically.

F. Very few people can control every facial movement. Most notably, actors and politicians may become skilled at hiding their real feelings. Even so, an emotion may briefly leak through before the person is conscious of it. Sadness is especially difficult to fake or conceal. When someone is truly sad, the forehead wrinkles with grief, and the inner corners of the eyebrows move upwards. In Ekman’s tests, fewer than 15 per cent of participants could make this eyebrow movement voluntarily. Anger is easier to imitate. The lowered eyebrows of an angry scowl can be replicated by almost everyone. Therefore, a person who claims to be sad but does not show raised inner eyebrows may not be expressing real sadness.

G. A smile is easier to counterfeit than sadness. Only two zygomaticus major muscles are needed to produce a false grin by pulling the corners of the lips upwards. A genuine smile involves more than the mouth. It also affects the orbicularis oculi, the muscle around the eye. This action produces the distinctive lines commonly called crow’s-feet. A false smile may be unmasked when the mouth rises but the surrounding eye area does not change naturally. In a real smile, the eyes may crinkle and the eyebrows may move slightly downwards. Without these signs, a false smile can appear unnatural and strained.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Aqua product: New Zealand's Algae Biodiesel

A. In May 2006, New Zealand's Aquaflow Bionomic Corporation announced a new biodiesel derived from sewage pond microalgae. The technology reached a major breakthrough in December 2007, when Massey University hosted the world's first public demonstration of this wild algae-based fuel. During the event, David Parker, Minister for Energy, successfully test-drove a Land Rover powered by Aquaflow's B5 blend, with politicians and media representatives in attendance. This successful trial confirmed the viability of wild algae as a low-cost, clean-energy feedstock for the country's future.

B. Algae-based biodiesel is anticipated to become an economical and cleaner fuel alternative for New Zealand's automobiles, with applications extending to boats, buses, heating systems, and power generation. A key advantage lies in supply: algae are available in abundance, thriving in nutrient-rich wastewater such as the settling ponds of Effluent Management Systems (EMS). They are both indigenous and renewable, capable of doubling their biomass within 24 hours under favourable conditions. Through photosynthesis, algae produce and store energy in the form of lipids and combustible elements — the same compounds Aquaflow is striving to extract at competitive cost. Industry analysts estimate that algae growing in optimised ponds can yield up to 5,000 tonnes of biomass per hectare annually, generating multiple beneficial byproducts.

C. The process began when Aquaflow agreed to commence a pilot project with Marlborough District Council in 2005, extracting algae from the council's 50-hectare Blenheim-based EMS ponds. By treating the primary contaminant of these ponds as a fuel feedstock, Aquaflow is simultaneously aiding the council's bioremediation process of cleaning up water discharge. The dual-purpose model carries significant cross-industry implications: dairy farmers, food-processing facilities, and municipal water-treatment authorities could each adopt the same methodology to reap revenue from waste streams that currently incur disposal costs. Estimates suggest that fewer than 200 participating farms nationally could yield enough algal biomass to supply 8 percent of New Zealand's diesel demand by 2015.

D. Compared with conventional biofuels, algal biodiesel offers measurable advantages. Corn-based ethanol typically requires 0.6 hectares of arable land per 1,000 litres produced, while soy-based biodiesel needs approximately 1.5 hectares for the same output. Algae cultivation, by contrast, occupies no agricultural land and yields between 10 and 100 times more oil per hectare than soy. Production economics also favour algae: industry projections place mature algal biodiesel at NZ$0.85 per litre, against NZ$1.20 for soy-derived biodiesel and NZ$1.05 for corn ethanol. Crucially, algae do not compete with food crops for arable land, water, or fertiliser, sidestepping the food-versus-fuel controversy that has dogged first-generation biofuels since the mid-2000s and prompted policy reviews in the European Union and the United States.

E. The biofuels are blended with mineral diesel rather than used in raw form, helping meet New Zealand's B5 target of 5 percent blending introduced in 2008. Aquaflow plans to augment its production capacity from current pilot-scale output to one million litres annually within the coming year, with a longer-term target of 50 million litres by 2015. The company is preparing a prospectus for potential investors before Christmas, aiming to woo capital for full commercial rollout. Independent carbon analysis suggests that algal biodiesel produces roughly 75 percent fewer net CO2 emissions over its full life cycle than fossil diesel — a credential the company actively highlights as evidence that the technology can contribute meaningfully to national emissions-reduction commitments under the Kyoto Protocol.

F. Not all observers share Aquaflow's optimism. Independent biofuel researchers have raised three principal concerns. First, scaling laboratory yields to industrial volumes has historically proven difficult; several international algae-fuel ventures failed to reach cost parity with fossil diesel between 2008 and 2012. Second, excessive algal blooms in untreated ponds may generate unbearable stench and tinting of water, creating environmental risks if extraction lags behind growth. Third, downstream refining of lipid-rich algae into transport-grade fuel remains energy-intensive, potentially offsetting the carbon advantage. A 2009 University of Auckland study concluded that algal biodiesel would become commercially viable only if extraction efficiency improved by 30 percent and feedstock collection became fully automated.

G. Beyond fuel, algae underpin an ethnic dietary tradition spanning continents — Japanese cuisine incorporates over 20 species, while Chinese cooking uses more than 70. Commercially cultivated strains, including Spirulina, Chlorella, and Dunaliella, are marketed as health supplements rich in B-vitamins, iodine, iron, and calcium. Algal pigments serve as an eco-friendly alternative to synthetic dyes, while seaweed-derived compounds are routinely processed as fertiliser or livestock feed. Aquaflow's invention is subject to a provisional patent that prevents competitors from using the technology illegally. From a sustainability perspective, the noticeable feature of algaculture is that growth inputs — wastewater, sunlight, and carbon dioxide — exist naturally in plentiful supply, making the complete production cycle a sustainable disposal route for organic effluent and a prominent component of broader aquaculture.

Industry analysts estimate that algae growing in optimised ponds can yield up to 5,000 tonnes of biomass per hectare annually, generating multiple beneficial byproducts.

C. The process began when Aquaflow agreed to commence a pilot project with Marlborough District Council in 2005, extracting algae from the council's 50-hectare Blenheim-based EMS ponds. By treating the primary contaminant of these ponds as a fuel feedstock, Aquaflow is simultaneously aiding the council's bioremediation process of cleaning up water discharge. The dual-purpose model carries significant cross-industry implications: dairy farmers, food-processing facilities, and municipal water-treatment authorities could each adopt the same methodology to reap revenue from waste streams that currently incur disposal costs. Estimates suggest that fewer than 200 participating farms nationally could yield enough algal biomass to supply 8 percent of New Zealand's diesel demand by 2015.

D. Compared with conventional biofuels, algal biodiesel offers measurable advantages. Corn-based ethanol typically requires 0.6 hectares of arable land per 1,000 litres produced, while soy-based biodiesel needs approximately 1.5 hectares for the same output. Algae cultivation, by contrast, occupies no agricultural land and yields between 10 and 100 times more oil per hectare than soy. Production economics also favour algae: industry projections place mature algal biodiesel at NZ$0.85 per litre, against NZ$1.20 for soy-derived biodiesel and NZ$1.05 for corn ethanol. Crucially, algae do not compete with food crops for arable land, water, or fertiliser, sidestepping the food-versus-fuel controversy that has dogged first-generation biofuels since the mid-2000s and prompted policy reviews in the European Union and the United States.

E. The biofuels are blended with mineral diesel rather than used in raw form, helping meet New Zealand's B5 target of 5 percent blending introduced in 2008. Aquaflow plans to augment its production capacity from current pilot-scale output to one million litres annually within the coming year, with a longer-term target of 50 million litres by 2015. The company is preparing a prospectus for potential investors before Christmas, aiming to woo capital for full commercial rollout. Independent carbon analysis suggests that algal biodiesel produces roughly 75 percent fewer net CO2 emissions over its full life cycle than fossil diesel — a credential the company actively highlights as evidence that the technology can contribute meaningfully to national emissions-reduction commitments under the Kyoto Protocol.

F. Not all observers share Aquaflow's optimism. Independent biofuel researchers have raised three principal concerns. First, scaling laboratory yields to industrial volumes has historically proven difficult; several international algae-fuel ventures failed to reach cost parity with fossil diesel between 2008 and 2012. Second, excessive algal blooms in untreated ponds may generate unbearable stench and tinting of water, creating environmental risks if extraction lags behind growth. Third, downstream refining of lipid-rich algae into transport-grade fuel remains energy-intensive, potentially offsetting the carbon advantage. A 2009 University of Auckland study concluded that algal biodiesel would become commercially viable only if extraction efficiency improved by 30 percent and feedstock collection became fully automated.

G. Beyond fuel, algae underpin an ethnic dietary tradition spanning continents — Japanese cuisine incorporates over 20 species, while Chinese cooking uses more than 70. Commercially cultivated strains, including Spirulina, Chlorella, and Dunaliella, are marketed as health supplements rich in B-vitamins, iodine, iron, and calcium. Algal pigments serve as an eco-friendly alternative to synthetic dyes, while seaweed-derived compounds are routinely processed as fertiliser or livestock feed. Aquaflow's invention is subject to a provisional patent that prevents competitors from using the technology illegally. From a sustainability perspective, the noticeable feature of algaculture is that growth inputs — wastewater, sunlight, and carbon dioxide — exist naturally in plentiful supply, making the complete production cycle a sustainable disposal route for organic effluent and a prominent component of broader aquaculture.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

Jean Piaget (1896–1980)

Seymour Papert looks at the work of the pioneering Swiss philosopher and psychologist

Jean Piaget spent much of his professional life listening to children, watching children and poring over reports of researchers around the world who were doing the same. He found, to put it most succinctly, that children don’t think like grown-ups. After thousands of interactions with young people often barely old enough to talk, Piaget began to suspect that behind their cute and seemingly irrational utterances were thought processes that had their own kind of order and their own special logic. Einstein called it “a discovery so simple that only a genius could have thought of it.”

Although not an educational reformer, Piaget championed a way of thinking about children that provided the foundation for today’s education-reform movements. It was a shift comparable to the way modern anthropology displaced stories of primitive tribes being ‘noble savages’ and ‘cannibals’. One might say that Piaget was the first to take children’s thinking seriously.

He has been revered by generations of teachers inspired by the belief that children are not empty vessels to be filled with knowledge [as traditional pedagogical theory had it] but active builders of knowledge—little scientists who are constantly creating and testing their own hypotheses about the world. And though he may not be as famous as Sigmund Freud or even B. F. Skinner, his influence on psychology may be longer lasting.

In 1920, while doing research in a child-psychology laboratory in Paris, Piaget noticed that children of the same age made similar errors on intelligence tests. Fascinated by their reasoning processes, he began to suspect that the key to human knowledge might be discovered by observing how the child’s mind develops. On his return to Switzerland he began watching children play, scrupulously recording their words and actions as their minds raced to find reasons for why things are the way they are. In one of his most famous experiments, Piaget asked children, ‘What makes the wind?’ A typical dialogue would be:

Piaget

What makes the wind?

Julia

The trees.

Piaget

How do you know?

Julia

I saw them waving their arms.

Piaget

How does that make the wind?

Julia

(waving her hand in front of his face)

Like this. Only they are bigger. And there are lots of trees.

Piaget recognised that five-year-old Julia’s beliefs, while not correct by any adult criterion, are not ‘incorrect’ either. They are entirely sensible and coherent within the framework of the child’s way of knowing. Classifying them as ‘true’ or ‘false’ misses the point and shows a lack of respect for the child. What Piaget was after was a theory that the wind dialogue demonstrated coherence, ingenuity and the practice of a kind of explanatory principle that stands young children in very good stead when they don’t know enough or don’t have enough skill to handle the kind of explanation that grown-ups prefer.

Piaget was not an educator and never laid down rules about how to intervene in such situations. But his work strongly suggests that the automatic reaction of putting the child right may well be counter-productive. If their theories are always greeted by ‘Nice try, but this is how it really is________’ they might give up after a while on making theories. As Piaget put it, ‘children have real understanding only of that which they invent themselves, and each time that we try to teach them something too quickly, we keep them from inventing it themselves.’

Disciples of Piaget have a tolerance for—indeed a fascination with—children’s primitive laws of physics: that things disappear when they are out of sight; that the moon and the sun follow you around; that big things float and small things sink. Einstein was intrigued by Piaget’s findings, especially by the idea that seven-year-olds insist that going faster can take more time—perhaps because this, like Einstein’s own theories of relativity, runs so contrary to common sense.

Although every teacher in training still memorises Piaget’s successive stages of childhood development, the greater part of Piaget’s work is less well known, perhaps because schools of education regard it as ‘too deep’ for teachers. Piaget never thought of himself as a child psychologist. His real interest was epistemology—the theory of knowledge—which, like physics, was considered a branch of philosophy until Piaget came along and made it a science.

Through epistemology, Piaget explored multiple ways of knowing. He acknowledged them and examined them non-judgementally, yet with a philosopher’s analytic rigour. Since Piaget, the territory has been widely colonised by those who write about women’s ways of knowing, Afrocentric ways of knowing, even the computer’s ways of knowing. Indeed, artificial intelligence and the information-processing model of the mind owe more to Piaget than its proponents may realise.

The core of Piaget is his belief that looking carefully at how knowledge develops in children will elucidate the nature of knowledge in general. Whether this has in fact led to deeper understanding remains, like everything about Piaget, controversial. In the past decade, Piaget has been vigorously challenged by the current fashion of viewing knowledge as an intrinsic property of the brain. Ingenious experiments have demonstrated that newborn infants already have some of the knowledge that Piaget believed children constructed. But for those, like me, who still see Piaget as the giant in the field of cognitive theory, the difference between what the baby brings and what the adult has is so immense that the new discoveries do not significantly reduce the gap, but only increase the mystery.
